title: When the Typewriter Turns
premise: In 1934, Coral Amberdale keeps the last manned lighthouse on a storm-battered coast, recording weather and ship traffic in an old typewriter salvaged from her late husband's office. When a census taker named Idris Vane arrives asking questions that have nothing to do with population counts, Coral discovers the government is quietly erasing the coastal villages slated for seizure under a new emergency decree — including the lighthouse itself. Together with the displaced villagers who shelter in her tower, Coral races to type out and smuggle a true record of the evictions to a dissident printer in the capital before the victors' historians can publish their sanitized version. The book ends with the lighthouse dark and demolished, but Coral's typed testimony hidden inside thousands of innocuous census forms, read aloud years later at a reckoning tribunal — proof that memory, once set down, cannot be fully confiscated.
about_author: Kestrel Vasquez is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging seized municipal records from coastal towns. They write historical fiction about ordinary people who refuse to let paperwork decide what really happened.

chapters.title: The Weight of What Stays
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. A routine winter of log entries, lamp oil, and grief, establishing how she measures her world — by what fits in two hands. The great storms begin early, and a fishing boat wrecks within sight of the light. Emotional beat: loneliness sharpened into competence; Coral is capable but unmoored.

chapters.title: A Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Census taker Idris Vane arrives soaked and apologetic, but his questions drift from household size to 'sentiment toward relocation.' Coral notices his form has no official seal. He leaves a carbon copy behind by accident — or on purpose. Emotional beat: unease; the first crack in the official story.

chapters.title: Villages That Aren't There
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. We see his conflict: he is meant to map what will be erased, not warn anyone. He compares his orders against shipping manifests and realizes three neighboring villages are already struck from maps. Emotional beat: guilt curdling into resolve as he chooses to return to the lighthouse.

chapters.title: Tenants of the Tower
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Evicted families arrive seeking shelter — the Okafor brothers, old Marta with her goat, a mute boy called Pip. The lighthouse becomes a crowded, quarrelsome found family. Coral resents them, then feeds them. Emotional beat: reluctant belonging; grief making room for others.

chapters.title: The Decree
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. He brings the emergency decree itself: the coast is to be seized for a naval installation, residents declared 'statistically negligible.' Coral recognizes the typewriter font on the decree matches her husband's old office machine — the state reuses its tools. Emotional beat: cold fury; power revealed as paperwork.

chapters.title: What the Logbook Knows
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She realizes her years of shipping logs contradict the official claim that the villages were 'already abandoned' before the storms. The typewriter becomes an instrument of witness. The group begins typing testimony onto blank census forms. Emotional beat: purpose; memory weaponized through mundane labor.

chapters.title: Storm Season
chapters.summary: Pip's POV, rendered in spare interior monologue. The worst storm of the year hits while inspectors arrive unexpectedly; the villagers hide in the lamp room as Coral keeps the light burning through the night for a foundering patrol boat — the same navy that will evict them. Emotional beat: terror and grace; saving the people sent to erase you.

chapters.title: The Confession of Idris Vane
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. Inspectors return, suspicious; Idris burns his real orders and signs his name to the villagers' testimony, making himself a co-conspirator. Marta dies during the raid, and her death becomes the record's first entry. Emotional beat: sacrifice; a bureaucrat finally accountable to something human.

chapters.title: Carried Out to Sea
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The climax: soldiers come to extinguish the light for good. The villagers smuggle the typed forms out in Marta's goat cart and a fishing skiff through the tail of the storm, while Coral stays behind to delay the officers with bureaucratic politeness. The lighthouse goes dark. Emotional beat: heartbreak and defiance; the truth escapes even as the home does not.

chapters.title: Read Into the Record
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs, years later. At a postwar tribunal, a clerk reads Coral's census-form testimony aloud; survivors in the gallery recognize their own words. Coral, older and living inland, hears her husband's typewriter rhythm echoed in the courtroom stenographer's keys. Emotional beat: vindication without restoration — memory survives, and that is enough.
